entities.summary:
Suwon, the capital of Gyeonggi Province, South Korea, has been a pivotal urban center since its establishment during the late Joseon Dynasty in the 14th century. Geographically positioned just south of Seoul, Suwon is renowned for its well-preserved Hwaseong Fortress, a UNESCO World Heritage site completed in 1796, which exemplifies advanced military architecture and urban planning of the period. The city played a crucial role in the development of Korean identity and culture, particularly during the tumultuous transitions of the 20th century as Korea faced Japanese colonization and subsequent division.

The construction of Hwaseong Fortress under King Jeongjo was not merely a defensive measure; it represented an architectural and cultural renaissance aimed at solidifying the central authority of the Joseon Dynasty. The fortress was innovative, incorporating Western military principles alongside traditional Korean designs. This project mobilized thousands of laborers and artisans, showcasing the era's technological advancements in construction and engineering. Furthermore, Suwon served as a political and administrative hub, where significant decisions were made that would influence the broader trajectory of Korean history.

In the aftermath of the Korean War, Suwon transformed into a center of industrial growth and urbanization, reflecting the broader economic development patterns of South Korea. The city has since evolved into a modern metropolis while maintaining its historical roots, becoming a symbol of resilience and cultural continuity. Its historical sites attract millions of visitors, fostering a sense of national pride and identity among Koreans.
